issues.legal_issue: The disappearance of a duly executed will does not, by itself, establish its revocation, and the objector must prove revocation in a legally recognized manner.
material_facts: The courts had found that the testatrix executed and registered the will while of sound disposing mind, without fraud or undue influence.
The original will was not found after her death, although a draft with substantially similar recitals was discovered.
The will reflected a clear disposition consistent with the testatrix’s earlier dispositions, including religious and charitable purposes and restrictions on alienation.
The testatrix’s relations with the objector were strained, and the record showed no change of intention or reason for her to revoke the will in the objector’s favour.
The objector and his wife had access to the testatrix’s house, and the evidence did not establish that she revoked the will by a legally recognized act.
issues.conclusion: The presumption of revocation, if any, was rebutted; the objector failed to prove revocation. The appeal was allowed, the probate application was granted, and the single judge’s decision was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 70 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, an unprivileged will may be revoked only by the specified methods, including a later will or qualifying writing, or by burning, tearing or otherwise destroying it with the required intention. The objector relying on revocation bears the burden of proving it. If a will last traced to the testator’s possession is missing at death, a presumption of revocation may arise depending on the circumstances, but it is weak, must be applied cautiously in light of Indian habits and conditions, and may be rebutted by slight direct or circumstantial evidence. A clear and consistent disposition, no apparent reason or change of intention supporting revocation, and the possibility of loss, misplacement or removal by an interested person may rebut the presumption. The Court relied on Anna Maria Welch v. Nathaniel Phillips, Padman v. Hanwanta, Finch v. Finch, Anil Behari Ghosh v. Smt. Latika Bala Dassi, and Kaikhushru Jehangir v. Bai Bachubai Jehangir, among other authorities.

rule.if: probate_proceeding and duly_executed_will_missing_at_death and clear_stable_disposition and no_evidence_of_changed_intention and no_proof_of_revocation_act and (interested_person_had_access or loss_or_removal_was_possible)

predicates.probate_proceeding: A party seeks probate or administration of a will whose validity or continued effect is contested.
predicates.duly_executed_will_missing_at_death: The will was duly executed but its original could not be found when the testator died.
predicates.clear_stable_disposition: The will made a clear disposition consistent with the testator’s established intentions and dispositions.
predicates.no_evidence_of_changed_intention: The evidence did not show a change in the testator’s intentions or a reason to revoke the will.
predicates.no_proof_of_revocation_act: The objector did not prove that the testator revoked the will by a legally recognized act.
predicates.interested_person_had_access: A person who would benefit from defeating the will had access to where it could have been kept.
predicates.loss_or_removal_was_possible: The circumstances left open the possibility that the will was lost, misplaced, stolen or removed by someone other than the testator.
predicates.revocation_not_established: The objector has not established that the will was revoked.

issues.definition: When a duly executed will is missing in a probate proceeding, a clear and stable disposition, no evidence of changed intention or a revocation act, and a plausible possibility of loss or removal mean that revocation is not established.
